findings.title: should_block? mutates and persists match stats as a side effect of validation, causing double counting
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and saves the record every time it is called. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which runs as part of `User` validations. `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168) explicitly calls `user.valid?` before calling `user.save` (line 172), and `save` internally re-runs validations. Because `email_changed?` is true for a brand-new unsaved user both times, validations (and therefore the BlockedEmail side effect) run twice for every single sign-up attempt against a blocked address, so `match_count` is incremented twice (and `last_match_at` recomputed twice) per attempt, corrupting the very statistics this feature is meant to track. The side effect is also persisted outside of the `User` save/transaction (validations run before the AR save transaction begins), so the counters are updated even if the `User` save subsequently fails, or if `valid?` is called anywhere else (forms, specs, console) without ever creating a user.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment risks lost updates under concurrent requests
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back without any locking or atomic SQL update. If two sign-up attempts for the same blocked email happen concurrently (a realistic scenario for exactly the kind of repeated spam/bot signups this feature targets), both requests can read the same starting value and each save overwrites the other's increment, silently losing hits/undercounting match_count. This should use an atomic update such as `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `match_count = match_count + 1`.

findings.title: Blocked email lookup and uniqueness are case-sensitive, allowing the block to be bypassed by case variation
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and the `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` on line 5 do no case normalization. Elsewhere in the app, email comparisons are explicitly case-normalized (e.g. `UsersController#change_email` uses `Email.downcase`), but `BlockedEmail` does not. As a result, an admin who blocks "Spammer@EXAMPLE.com" will fail to block a sign-up using "spammer@example.com" (or any other casing variant), defeating the purpose of the feature. It also permits multiple rows for the same logical address differing only in case, since the uniqueness check is case-sensitive by default.

findings.title: rejectedEmails default array literal is shared across controller instances and never reset
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a single array object as the default value directly on the controller definition instead of creating a fresh array per instance (e.g. via `init`). In Ember, object/array literals used as defaults this way are shared by reference across every instance created from the same class/mixin definition rather than instantiated per object — a well known Ember pitfall. Because the array is also never cleared anywhere (no reset on modal open/close or `init`), once an email is pushed into `rejectedEmails` it stays rejected for the lifetime of that shared array object. If the "Create Account" controller is ever recreated (e.g. the modal reopened, or in a shared/kiosk browser session), a previously rejected email — even from an unrelated earlier attempt, or one that the server would no longer reject (e.g. an admin unblocked it) — will continue to be permanently flagged invalid client-side with no way to retry short of a full page reload.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist validation behavior has no test coverage after being moved into EmailValidator
findings.body: The domain-restriction logic (`email_in_restriction_setting?` plus the whitelist/blacklist branches) was moved out of `User` (previously `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?`, deleted from app/models/user.rb in this PR) into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only covers the new "blocked email" branch via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and adds no example for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior, so this pre-existing, non-trivial logic is left untested after the refactor. Additionally, any prior spec that exercised the now-removed `User#email_validator`/`User#email_in_restriction_setting?` methods directly would fail since those methods no longer exist on `User`.

findings.title: action_type column has no DB default or range validation, relying only on an app-level callback
findings.body: The `action_type` column is declared `null: false` with no database default, and the only place a default is applied is the `before_validation :set_defaults` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb (lines 21-23), which only runs through ActiveRecord's validation path. There is also no validation constraining `action_type` to the two defined enum values (`actions[:block]`/`actions[:do_nothing]`). The spec file's own comment ("If we manually load the table with some emails...") suggests bulk/manual loading is an expected use case; such inserts bypassing ActiveRecord callbacks would violate the NOT NULL constraint unless `action_type` is explicitly supplied, and any out-of-range value stored would silently be treated as "do nothing" by `should_block?`'s equality check rather than raising an error.
